hero.heading: Myotherapy in Melbourne
hero.subheading: Hands-on treatment for tight, sore muscles and soft tissue, with a proper assessment behind it—so you find out why it keeps tightening, not just that it does.

intro.heading: When your body keeps holding on
paragraphs: Your neck and upper traps are hard as a rock by Wednesday. Headaches start at the base of your skull and creep forward. Your calves and glutes will not let go, no matter how much you foam roll. Your lower back feels more tight than painful, until one morning it is not. Maybe you have caught yourself clenching your jaw at your desk.
Or you book a monthly massage that feels amazing and lasts about four days.

That relief is real, and it is worth having. But if the same tightness comes back on the same schedule, something is usually loading that tissue. That is worth finding, and it is where myotherapy starts.

explainer.heading: What is myotherapy?
paragraphs: Myotherapy is the assessment and treatment of musculoskeletal pain and dysfunction that comes from muscles and soft tissue: the muscles, fascia, tendons and connective tissue that let you move.

Myotherapists train through an advanced diploma of myotherapy or a bachelor of health science in clinical myotherapy. Unlike our osteopaths, physiotherapists and chiropractors, myotherapists are not registered through AHPRA. The profession is self-regulated through professional associations, and we would rather say that plainly. See how each of our disciplines is qualified on our qualifications page.

A session may include soft tissue and deep tissue techniques, trigger point therapy, myofascial techniques, dry needling, joint mobilisation, stretching, taping and home advice. When people talk about “knots”, they usually mean trigger points: small, tender, tight spots within a muscle that can feel sore when pressed and sometimes send discomfort elsewhere.

What sets myotherapy apart is the assessment. Your myotherapist tests how you move, checks range of motion and looks at the tissue involved, then builds a working explanation of why it is behaving the way it is.

Myotherapy or remedial massage? Both are hands-on soft tissue treatments, and both can help a tight back feel better. Remedial massage therapists typically train to diploma level and focus on treating the tissue presented. Myotherapists train for longer, use a broader set of techniques including dry needling, and add an assessment step aimed at the source of the problem as well as its site. If you want a good treatment for a tight back, either can help. If you want someone to work out why the same back keeps tightening, myotherapy is set up for that.

What about dry needling? Dry needling places fine, single-use filament needles into trigger points within a muscle. It uses the same kind of needle as acupuncture but different reasoning: dry needling is based on a Western musculoskeletal framework, while acupuncture comes from traditional Chinese medicine. Most people feel a brief twitch or a deep ache, and next-day soreness similar to a hard training session is common. Bruising can occur, and like any needle-based technique there are less common risks, which your myotherapist will explain first. It is always optional, and you can have a full treatment without it.

visit.heading: Your first myotherapy appointment
visit.intro: A clear, conversational process with no surprises.

steps.title: Tell us what is going on
steps.copy: We ask about your symptoms, your history, your work and training, and what you want to get back to.

steps.title: Move through an assessment
steps.copy: Your myotherapist checks how you move and the tissue involved, and explains what they notice.

steps.title: Agree on treatment
steps.copy: Options, including whether dry needling is suitable for you, are explained before hands-on care begins.

steps.title: Leave with a plan
steps.copy: You will usually leave with stretches, exercises or advice to keep things moving between visits.

notes.title: Come in comfortable clothes
notes.copy: Activewear or loose clothing works well, so we can reach the area and see how you move.

notes.title: You set the pressure
notes.copy: Firm does not have to mean painful. Tell us what feels okay and we will adjust.

notes.title: Expect some soreness
notes.copy: Feeling sore for a day or two is common, especially after deep tissue work or dry needling.

team.heading: Clinically trained, part of the wider team
team.copy: Our myotherapists work alongside Alpha's osteopaths, physiotherapists, chiropractors and exercise physiologists, with the same approach: listen properly, assess first and explain clearly. You can find each myotherapist's qualifications on our team page.

faqs.question: What is the difference between myotherapy and remedial massage?
faqs.answer: Both are hands-on soft tissue treatments. Myotherapists complete longer training, use a broader range of techniques including dry needling, and assess where a problem may be coming from as well as where you feel it. Remedial massage is a good option with a different scope.

faqs.question: Can I claim myotherapy on private health?
faqs.answer: You may be able to. Cover for myotherapy depends on your fund, your level of extras cover and the myotherapist's professional association membership. Check with your fund before your appointment.

faqs.question: Do I need a referral?
faqs.answer: No. You can book a myotherapist directly without a GP referral.

faqs.question: Does it hurt, and will I be sore afterwards?
faqs.answer: Some techniques feel firm or tender, especially on tight areas, and we will work within what is comfortable for you. Soreness for a day or two afterwards is common, a bit like after a hard training session. If anything feels unusual or does not settle, let us know or speak with your GP.

faqs.question: What is dry needling, and do I have to have it?
faqs.answer: Dry needling places fine, single-use needles into trigger points within a muscle. It can cause a twitch, a deep ache and next-day soreness, and bruising is possible. It is always optional: your myotherapist will explain it, check it is suitable for you and only go ahead with your consent.

faqs.question: How often should I come?
faqs.answer: It depends on what is going on and what you want. Some people book regular maintenance sessions; others want to understand why a problem keeps returning. Your myotherapist will suggest a plan after your assessment and review it with you.

faqs.question: Should I book myotherapy, or see an osteo or physio first?
faqs.answer: If your main concern is tight, sore muscles, myotherapy is a reasonable place to start. If you have had a recent injury, or your pain is sharp, worsening or spreading, an osteopath or physiotherapist may be a better first step. If you are not sure, tell us what is going on and we will point you to the right person. For new or unexplained symptoms, your GP is always a good place to start.

faqs.question: What should I wear?
faqs.answer: Comfortable clothing you can move in, such as activewear. We may need access to the area being treated, and we will always explain what we are doing and check you are comfortable first.

closing.heading: Get hands-on care, and find out why
closing.copy: Book a myotherapy appointment for hands-on treatment and a clear explanation of what is going on. Not sure it is the right service? Tell us what is happening and we will help you find the right fit.
